name: Inherited Disorders of Amino Acid Metabolism in Adults

clinicalPearls: Disorders of amino acid metabolism are individually rare (roughly 1 in 10,000 to 1 in 200,000) but collectively affect around 1 in 4000 newborns, and nearly all are inherited as autosomal recessive traits.

Conditions are generally named for the compound that accumulates to highest concentration: aminoacidopathies show excess of the parent amino acid, whereas organic acidemias accumulate downstream catabolic products.

Some defects (e.g., sarcosinemia, cystathioninuria, hyperlysinemia) are clinically benign, while at the opposite extreme complete ornithine transcarbamylase deficiency is lethal in the untreated neonate.

Classic phenylketonuria results from deficient phenylalanine hydroxylase activity; untreated infants are normal at birth but develop microcephaly, progressive intellectual disability, seizures, hypopigmentation, eczema, and a characteristic mousy odor from phenylacetate.

Classic homocystinuria (cystathionine beta-synthase deficiency) typically presents at 3-5 years with dislocated optic lenses, intellectual disability in about half, marfanoid habitus, and osteoporosis, with total plasma homocysteine usually above 100 micromol/L.

Alkaptonuria (homogentisate 1,2-dioxygenase deficiency) may be unrecognized until midlife; urine darkens on standing or with alkali, and ochronotic pigment deposits cause degenerative arthritis, scleral and ear pigmentation, and later aortic stenosis.
Ornithine transcarbamylase deficiency is X-linked and the most common urea cycle defect; heterozygous females can become symptomatic when mutant hepatocytes predominate due to random X-inactivation.

Plasma citrulline helps localize urea cycle defects: it is low or undetectable in proximal defects (NAGS, CPS-1, OTC) and markedly elevated in citrullinemia type 1 (argininosuccinate synthase deficiency).
Urine orotic acid is increased only in ornithine transcarbamylase deficiency among the proximal urea cycle defects, distinguishing it from CPS-1 and N-acetylglutamate synthase deficiency.
Diagnosis relies on plasma amino acid analysis, urine organic acid analysis (GC/MS), and plasma acylcarnitine profile (tandem MS), confirmed by enzyme assay or DNA testing.
Some metabolic disorders remain asymptomatic until adulthood, declaring themselves only when fasting or severe stress demands full activity of the affected pathway.

In maternal phenylketonuria, uncontrolled maternal phenylalanine levels before and during pregnancy increase fetal risk of congenital defects, microcephaly, intellectual disability, and growth retardation regardless of fetal genotype.
harrison.pathophysiology: Each amino acid has a unique degradative pathway that recycles its nitrogen and carbon for synthesis of other amino acids, carbohydrates, and lipids. An enzymatic block causes accumulation of compounds upstream of the lesion; what accumulates depends on the site of the block, reversibility of proximal reactions, and availability of alternative metabolic runoff pathways. In phenylketonuria, accumulated phenylalanine competitively inhibits transport of other amino acids needed for protein and neurotransmitter synthesis, reduces myelin synthesis while increasing its degradation, impairs norepinephrine and serotonin formation, and inhibits tyrosinase causing hypopigmentation. In homocystinuria, defective cystathionine beta-synthase or impaired remethylation of homocysteine to methionine raises homocysteine, which produces endothelial dysfunction and acts as an atherogenic and thrombophilic agent. In urea cycle defects, ammonia generated from protein nitrogen cannot be cleared, so ammonia and glutamine accumulate causing direct neuronal toxicity and brain edema. In alkaptonuria, deficient homogentisate 1,2-dioxygenase leads to urinary excretion of homogentisic acid and deposition of its oxidized pigment in connective tissue (ochronosis).
additionalDifferentials: Phenylketonuria versus the cofactor (tetrahydrobiopterin-related) hyperphenylalaninemias such as DHPR, PTPS, and GTP cyclohydrolase 1 deficiencies
Classic cystathionine beta-synthase homocystinuria versus remethylation defects (methionine synthase / cblE, cblG) and combined methylmalonic acidemia-homocystinuria (cblC, D, F, J)
Urea cycle defects distinguished among each other by plasma citrulline, arginine, and urine orotic acid patterns
Ochronotic arthritis of alkaptonuria versus rheumatoid arthritis (small joints typically spared in ochronosis)
infectionMimics: Nonspecific hepatitis can be misdiagnosed in urea cycle defects presenting with hepatic dysfunction
nonInfectiousMimics: Gastrointestinal disorders, food allergies, and behavioral problems are common misdiagnoses in milder urea cycle defects with protein aversion and recurrent vomiting
Acquired hyperammonemia from liver disease of any cause, organic acidemias, or fatty acid oxidation defects can mimic urea cycle defects
Marfan syndrome can mimic the marfanoid habitus and lens dislocation of classic homocystinuria
additionalInvestigations: Quantitative plasma amino acid analysis (ion-exchange or LC/tandem MS)
Urine organic acid analysis by GC/MS
Plasma acylcarnitine profile by tandem mass spectrometry
Plasma ammonia and plasma glutamine measurement in suspected urea cycle defects
Urine orotic acid to differentiate OTC from CPS-1 and NAGS deficiency
Total plasma homocysteine and methionine for the homocystinurias
Urine organic acid analysis to identify homogentisic acid in alkaptonuria
Enzyme assay on cells/tissues or confirmatory DNA testing
Newborn screening (blood phenylalanine, methionine) with confirmatory metabolic testing for positive screens
redFlags: Neonate with refusal to feed and lethargy progressing to coma (classic urea cycle defect presentation at 1-4 days of life)
Hyperammonemia precipitated by systemic corticosteroids or chemotherapy, which can be fatal in previously asymptomatic individuals of any age
Postpartum behavioral change, stupor, or coma in a female (possible decompensated OTC deficiency from fasting and stress)
Life-threatening coronary, renal, or cerebral arterial thrombosis in a young patient with homocystinuria
Aortic stenosis developing in alkaptonuria, especially after age 60, from pigment deposition in heart valves
harrison.prognosis: Clinical manifestations of many of these conditions can be prevented or mitigated when diagnosis is early and appropriate management (e.g., dietary protein/amino acid restriction or vitamin supplementation) is started promptly; for phenylketonuria, treatment must begin before 2 weeks of age to prevent intellectual disability, and children detected and treated at birth show none of the classic abnormalities. Untreated classic disorders carry severe outcomes, including lethality of complete neonatal OTC deficiency and early vascular morbidity/mortality in homocystinuria. Alkaptonuria progresses slowly to disabling ochronotic arthritis and later cardiac valve disease.
pitfalls: Milder variants of homocystinuria may be missed by newborn methionine screening.
Heterozygous females with X-linked OTC deficiency can be overlooked because symptoms depend on the proportion of mutant hepatocytes from random X-inactivation.

Adult-onset metabolic decompensation can be triggered by involuntary fasting, severe stress, corticosteroids, or chemotherapy and may be mistaken for primary GI, allergic, behavioral, or hepatic disease.

Hyperhomocysteinemia has many acquired causes (B6/folate/B12 deficiency, aging, smoking, renal failure, hypothyroidism, leukemias, and certain drugs such as methotrexate, nitrous oxide, and isoniazid) that must be distinguished from inherited homocystinuria.

An abnormal newborn screen in an infant may actually reflect a maternal metabolic disorder (e.g., glutaric acidemia type 1, methylcrotonyl-CoA carboxylase deficiency, primary carnitine deficiency, fatty acid oxidation defect).
harrison.severityClassification: Severity is largely biochemical and enzyme-activity dependent: complete enzyme deficiencies (e.g., classic urea cycle defects) present catastrophically in the neonatal period, whereas partial/residual-activity variants may remain asymptomatic until adulthood and declare during fasting or stress. For phenylketonuria, dietary restriction is generally instituted when blood phenylalanine exceeds 360 micromol/L, with a target maintenance range of 120-360 micromol/L for life.
management: Treat phenylketonuria with a lifelong phenylalanine-restricted diet and amino acid supplements, adding the cofactor sapropterin in responsive patients or the enzyme substitute pegvaliase
Manage homocystinuria by trialling pyridoxine, with a methionine-restricted diet, cysteine supplementation, and betaine to lower homocysteine in non-responders, plus folate and vitamin B12
In alkaptonuria, reduce homogentisic acid production with nitisinone and moderate dietary protein, managing the resulting ochronotic arthropathy
For urea cycle defects, restrict dietary protein and use nitrogen-scavenging agents with arginine or citrulline supplementation
Treat acute metabolic decompensation and hyperammonaemia with protein withdrawal, intravenous glucose, scavenger therapy and haemodialysis when severe
Monitor metabolic control with serial plasma amino acid and ammonia measurement and screen for disease-specific complications such as lens dislocation and thromboembolism in homocystinuria
Provide genetic counselling and family screening for these autosomal recessive disorders and coordinate care with a metabolic specialist and dietitian
